translations.text: The enemy of truth saw the Lord and Savior, the life-giving God, being proclaimed, and was troubled.
He saw the Lord’s arrival on a donkey, glorified by us as before, and tried to stir up turmoil with the clatter of rattling chariots, to impede the donkey’s advance.
With its gently moving, steadily walking feet, it thwarted the warriors’ chariot horses. For he knew that the donkey had been prepared to defeat the chariots and horses.
For the Savior came on a donkey, not to display any weakness, but the gentleness of humility, so that he might extinguish arrogance.
And because the enemy knew that these things would happen according to the prophetic declaration, he became jealous and bore a grudge against the donkey.
But this was to extinguish the pride of the one who had become proud, and to humble the immense arrogance of the one who exalted himself in chariots and horses.
The blessed prophet had fittingly announced this beforehand and offered encouragement, saying: “Do not fear, daughter of Zion. Proclaim and rejoice, daughter of Jerusalem,
for behold, your king comes riding on a donkey’s colt, to destroy the chariots of Ephraim and the horses of Jerusalem.”
Do you see how he softened and brought down swaggering arrogance through gentleness? Just as he removed sufferings through suffering and bound death through death,
and exposed the adversary’s power to shame through the wood of the holy cross, so also through the donkey he demolished the horse-borne arrogance of the one who had grown boastful.
“Rejoice,” says the prophet, “daughter of Zion; exult and proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem.”
For it is right and fitting for those who worship God not only to possess the divine gifts themselves, but also to spread the proclamation of his goodness to others.
For behold, your king comes, gentle and humble, and seated on a donkey.
He fittingly placed “gentle” and “humble” first, to make clear that these were not signs of poverty, but tidings of gentleness and humility.
For if someone rides on a young donkey because he lacks possessions and has no horses, this is not counted as goodness or humility,
since the constraint of poverty brings him to this. But if someone who has chariots and many horses sits on a donkey’s colt out of gentleness, he adorns the practice of gentleness with humility.
The King of hosts did not lack chariots. The Only-begotten did not lack chariots and horses.

Of him the prophet says: “The chariots of God are tens of thousands, and thousands are their drivers.” He did not lack chariots, he who harnesses the winds and races along with wondrous and extraordinary reins.
Or do you not know how horses serve as mounts for us? As David says: “He who travels upon the wings of the winds.”
Thus he came on a donkey both to demolish arrogance through humility and to proclaim fully the foreshadowing of the Gentiles’ entry.
For the donkey is counted among the unclean animals, since Moses distinguished and set apart among the unclean animals everything that does not have a divided hoof and does not chew the cud.
And the donkey, because it neither chews the cud nor has a divided hoof, is counted among the unclean animals.
He was fulfilling beforehand the foreshadowings of his care that seeks out humanity, for he was going to call the [?] holy people a steed.
For just as horses are steeds for riding, so the souls of the saints are steeds for riders; so also the souls of the saints are steeds for God, for conduct and instructive commands,
according to what the prophet says: “You will mount your horses, and your riding is salvation.”
Paul was such an unruly, unbridled horse, disobedient to the divine laws.
He grazed in the pastures of the Law and kicked against the graces of the gospel. When the Son, the Lord of all, put a bridle on him and mounted him, he said:
“Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad and to kick against the sword.”
And since the colt has run away from the course of this discourse, let us implore the Lord of the colt, who is able to hold it, lead it, and keep it within the discourse.
For he is the one of whom the prophecy says, “He will bind his colt to the vine.”
Jesus sat on a colt—he who sits upon the cherubim, who above is awesome because of his divine nature, and below is longed for because of his grace and love for humanity.
The seraphim worship him with trembling in the heights, and he is proclaimed boldly on earth by us who are in the flesh.
For just as his birth above is awe-inspiring, so below the shoot that springs up of itself is longed for.
Jesus sat on a colt, and the crowds spread their garments before him. The honor was [?], but the honor offered by those honoring him was in no way worthy according to the commandment.
For God does not ask people for gifts according to his own worthiness, but according to the means of those honoring him.
Indeed, there is nothing at all that could honor God according to his own worthiness.
Neither all the earth, nor the whole heaven cast into voices, nor all the voices of angels and archangels,
nor tongues filled with things visible and invisible are sufficient to glorify him according to his own worthiness.
He rode on a colt, he who sits eternally in the heavens. People spread their garments before him, though they ought to have spread out their souls before their garments.
You who spread out your garments for the colt to tread upon, spread out your soul for God to dwell in.
This is also what John the Baptist proclaimed: “Prepare the ways of the Lord, and make the [?] paths straight.”
This means making souls ready, so that God and the Lord’s Son may enter and dwell in them.
Taking palm branches, they went out to meet him. And the children too blessed the one whom the angels glorify in heaven with fear,
rejoicing on earth and saying, “Hosanna!” In the Hebrew language this signifies glorification and great praise.
